ThreatSpire is one of the most thoughtfully designed platforms I’ve used for OT and SCADA threat intelligence. What stands out immediately is how well it understands the realities of industrial environments. Instead of forcing IT-style indicators onto control networks, it focuses on protocol-aware behavior and high-fidelity deception. The honeypot sensors that impersonate real equipment — Modicon PLCs, SIPROTEC relays, SIMATIC devices, and others — are excellent. They’re capture-only, so there’s no risk of them interfering with production systems, and the ability to switch vendor personas quickly makes them far more believable to an adversary conducting reconnaissance. The console itself feels built for practitioners. Actor tracking is clean and continuously updated, the AI-generated threat actor reports are grounded in actual evidence with source citations (not vague summaries), and the emphasis on turning intelligence into durable detections is exactly what most OT teams need. The recent “SCADA Threat Intel” blog series does a particularly good job explaining how to move from adversary profiles to protocol-level detections that survive normal operations — new peers, unexpected function codes, timing anomalies, and maintenance-window violations. That’s practical, high-value content. I also appreciate the evidence-first philosophy and MITRE ATT&CK-native approach. In critical infrastructure, you need to be able to defend every conclusion you present to operations or leadership. ThreatSpire makes that easier. Overall, this is a strong, purpose-built platform for anyone responsible for defending SCADA, power, manufacturing, or other OT environments. It bridges the gap between raw adversary intelligence and detections that actually work in the field. Highly recommended.

To the AI cyber naysayers who don’t see activity in their logs and discount increased AI cyber capacity:  I agree that we have not seen the science-fiction version of AI cyber risk materialize. Google Threat Intelligence says it has not observed AI giving APTs a “breakthrough capability” that changes the threat landscape.  But that is very different from saying attacker capability has not increased.  Anthropic analyzed 832 malicious accounts from March 2025–March 2026 and found AI being used across all 14 MITRE ATT&CK tactics and 482 sub-techniques. It documented attackers using AI for malware development, credential dumping, lateral movement, exploitation and web shells. The proportion of actors it classified medium-risk or above increased from 33% to 56%.  More importantly, these aren’t all lab demonstrations. Anthropic documented a real extortion operator targeting at least 17 organizations who used Claude Code for chained reconnaissance, exploitation, lateral movement and exfiltration while making operational decisions.  They’ve even documented ransomware development by an actor assessed as having only basic programming ability.  Google also reports state-backed actors using LLMs operationally for technical research, targeting, reconnaissance and rapidly producing sophisticated phishing lures.   Microsoft reports AI-automated phishing and acceleration of attack workflows.  So I wouldn’t argue that AI has suddenly created superhuman hackers. The evidence doesn’t support that.  But I also don’t think the evidence supports “nothing has changed.”  The measurable change is uplift: reduced skill requirements, increased throughput, faster reconnaissance and development, better social-engineering production, and increasingly autonomous orchestration of previously human-driven attack steps.

AIが危険かどうかを巡る論争が最近またにぎやかになっているが、今日の実際のニュースを見ると、そっちよりずっと具体的な話がある。「本質的に権力を集中させる技術だ」対「印刷機やインターネットと同じで分散させるべきだ」という構図は繰り返し起きていて、それはそれで面白い。ただ同じ日に、GoogleのMandiantがAIエージェントを使って2日で100件超の重大脆弱性を発見したという話を公開していた。理論の話は続いているが、実際に動いているものも増えている。  1. GoogleのMandiantが、社内で10ヶ月稼働させていたAIエージェントツール「AVDH（Agentic Vulnerability Discovery Harness）」の仕組みを公開した。脅威モデリング→エントリーポイント発見→コンテキスト収集→仮説生成→検証という専門エージェントのパイプラインで動作し、数千万行のコードをスキャンしてきた。ある調査では2日で100件超の重大脆弱性を発見し、これまでに12件のCVEが割り当てられている。 helpnetsecurity.com/2026/08/…  2. 日本政府の専門パネルが、生成AI企業に学習データと収集手法の開示を求める「原則コード」草案を承認した。「comply or explain（順守か説明か）」方式で、準拠しない場合は公表理由の説明が求められる。日本でAIサービスを提供する外国企業も対象となり、2025年5月成立のAI関連法に基づく措置。EU AI Actが8月2日から本格施行に入ったばかりのタイミングでもある。 japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0…  3. CerebrasがCS-4を発表した。ネットワークスイッチを排除し、ウェーハスケールプロセッサをラック間で直接接続する設計が特徴。前世代CS-3の最大2倍高速で、GPU比でユーザーあたり推論速度が最大30倍に達するとしている。ウェーハ間遅延を2マイクロ秒まで圧縮し、スイッチ層を消すことでAIクラスターのコストと消費電力を大きく削減できると説明する。 networkworld.com/article/421…  Yann LeCun（Meta）が、Anthropicの「AIは本質的に権力を集中させる」「オープンモデルはチップを持つ者への権力移動に過ぎない」という立場に対し、自身のXで「AIは印刷機やインターネットと同様、知識へのアクセスを改善して人間の知性を増幅させる。社会には多様なAIシステムが必要で、一つの企業が制御すべきではない」と反論した。投資家のGavin BakerやDavid Sacksも加わり、Anthropicの規制スタンスへの批判として広がっている。なお、この論争のきっかけとなったBakerの「Amodeiが内部で最後に残る唯一の民間企業になり得ると述べた」という主張は、Anthropicの研究者が否定している。 the-decoder.com/anthropic-ce…  今日一番手触りがあったのはMandiantのAVDHの話だ。10ヶ月動かし続けて、2日で100件の脆弱性を見つけた。地味な数字だが、積み重ねとして読むとそれなりの重みがある。LeCunとAnthropicの論争に「正解」があるとは思っていないが、その間に日本は開示コードを書き、Cerebrasはスイッチを消した。理論が定まる前に、現実が先に動いていく。それがここ最近ずっと続いている気がする。

Unpredictable, maybe ? 🤔 like an LLM on a Conputer can essentially do most of the things a human on a computer could do and for decades we‘ve heard „War Games“ like horror stories of thermonuclear war and „Atacks“ on Nuclear Power Plants and Hospitals and I honestly have no clue how people think that would even work. Like it’s not like nuclear submarine ICBM launch systems are connected to the public internet or that an operator in a nuclear power plant could just Homer Simpson like press the „Blow it up“ button and certainly there is no way to do so remotely…. And whenever you challenge this point „cyberwar“ experts will inevitably bring up Stuxnet which involved software, sure, but was a multi-year operation that would not have been possible without HumInt (by the way while @tracyalloway absolutely destroyed you at the opening of the episode (What the Hell did you do to her to deserve that ?) she failed to point out that rebranding AI as Intelligence would utterly confuse the Senate Appropriations Committee and that there already is a rather exclusive „Intelligence Community“ that might not own the copyright on the term (not that OpenAI or Anthropic would care) but that’s quite capable of protecting their turf.) and Stuxnet isn’t really a good illustration of a pure cyber-operation and in any case would far exceed the context window or runtime of any current LLM Agent even if it were. Generally most real cyberattacks take place over extended periods and could cause limited harm if discovered within a few days. So unless you „forgot“ to turn off your agents at the end of the test run the risk of that happening is rather minute. Just to clarify the timeframe is not related to lazy attackers but to actions the targets have to make to allow escalation into the next level so „superhuman“ speed doesn’t change anything about them. So Hospitals maybe ??? But like, Doctors are unlikely to just go home and leave their patients on the OR-Table because the IT system stoppef working… The most realistic attack surface for a consequential cyberattack would be financial systems but aside from crypto-world those systems are pretty secure and battle tested and even if you manage to transfer a couple of billions from BoA it’s not like that transaction could not just be reversed. The real world cybersecurity risk of LLMs are more about helping elevate threats from common criminals who now don‘t have to coerce a pro-level hacker to help them anymore. Those kinds of threats would involve both cyber and real world components. They are not categorically novel and law enforcement, in principle, knows how to deal with them and I‘m sure Palantir et al will have products to do so more efficiently if volumes increase. Cars, however, maim and kill people every day. They are extremely dangerous machines even with numerous safety features and in order to be able to continue to use them without incurring so many fatalities we‘ve had to introduce the novel legal concept of DUI and essentially restrict an activity older than human civilization, drinking, to areas where you can order an uber. While a limited rollout might rationally come with limited risks, the corporate PR risk is gigantic. So for a Company like Google to do it, they needed to take extraordinary precautions and ensure it‘s 102% safe. They pulled that off. They also have never produced a OpenAI/HF incident but that’s not because of their superior ability (they do have by far the best engineers in the industry though) and rather more related to being a mature business that’s less interested in grabbing attention than in not drawing scrutiny from regulators.

Superstition Rebellion: An Ethical, Logic-Driven Approach to Astrology  Astrology has occupied a complicated position in Indian society for centuries. For millions of people, Jyotish is connected with culture, spirituality, family traditions and the search for meaning during uncertain moments in life. At the same time, the modern astrology marketplace has also produced practices that can exploit fear, vulnerability and desperation. Predictions of unavoidable disasters, claims that a particular planet will destroy a person’s life, demands for expensive rituals, or promises of guaranteed wealth and miraculous cures can transform a traditional system of interpretation into a mechanism of psychological pressure. Against this background, the idea of a “superstition rebellion” represents a different direction: retaining the cultural and philosophical value of astrology while rejecting manipulation, fatalism and fear-based consultation.  Pandit Ajay Gautam has publicly positioned his astrological practice around this distinction. His AstroZon profile describes ethical practice, transparency and honesty as central principles and specifically states that astrology should offer guidance rather than function as a “magic wand.” His published material also says that he does not promote superstition and emphasizes karma correction rather than blind ritual. These are claims made by Gautam and his own platform, rather than independent scientific findings about the accuracy of astrology, but they provide a clear picture of the professional philosophy he presents to the public.  The central idea behind an ethical approach to astrology is remarkably simple: a person seeking guidance should leave a consultation with greater clarity, not greater fear. An astrologer may interpret a birth chart according to the principles of a particular astrological tradition, discuss periods of difficulty, identify traditionally significant planetary combinations, and suggest practices that the client considers meaningful. But there is an important ethical boundary between interpretation and intimidation. Saying that a chart contains a challenging period is fundamentally different from telling a frightened person that catastrophe is certain unless money is immediately paid for a ritual, gemstone or spiritual intervention.  This distinction becomes especially important because people generally approach astrologers at moments when they are searching for certainty. Someone worried about marriage, employment, business, family conflict or financial instability may be emotionally vulnerable. A prediction delivered with absolute authority can therefore influence major decisions. Ethical astrology must recognize this power imbalance. The astrologer may possess greater technical knowledge of the astrological system, but the client remains the person responsible for his or her life. Consultation should strengthen that agency rather than replace it.  A logic-driven approach does not necessarily require abandoning astrology. Instead, it requires being precise about what astrology can and cannot legitimately claim. Astrology is traditionally presented as an interpretive framework based on celestial positions, birth charts, planetary periods, transits and symbolic relationships. Gautam’s own published explanation of the astrologer’s role describes birth charts, Dashas and Gochar as important tools for interpreting life cycles. A responsible practitioner can work within that traditional framework while still acknowledging uncertainty and avoiding claims that exceed the evidence.  This distinction is particularly important because astrology and modern empirical science operate according to different standards of knowledge. Astrology has deep historical, cultural and philosophical traditions, but many specific predictive claims made by astrology have not been established as scientifically reliable. An ethical astrologer therefore should not present astrological interpretation as a medically proven diagnostic system, a guaranteed financial forecasting mechanism or a scientifically established method for determining the future. Respect for tradition and respect for intellectual honesty can coexist.  The phrase “superstition rebellion” can therefore be understood not as an attack on spirituality but as a rejection of exploitation carried out in the name of spirituality. Superstition becomes particularly problematic when uncertainty is converted into fear and fear is converted into commercial dependence. A person may be told that an invisible planetary danger is responsible for every problem in life and that only the astrologer possesses the special power to remove it. Such a relationship can gradually undermine independent judgment. A healthier consultation gives the client information, perspective and options without creating psychological dependency.  Pandit Ajay Gautam’s public material repeatedly emphasizes this non-fear-based philosophy. One of his published articles describes ethical guidance as providing honest predictions without fear-based tactics and presents practical remedies as solutions intended to have meaning in everyday life. His profile also describes remedies such as mantras, gemstones, rituals and lifestyle adjustments, while emphasizing that these should be approached as holistic guidance rather than as miraculous interventions.  The concept of a “remedy” itself deserves careful examination. In traditional Indian astrology, remedies can include mantra, charity, prayer, meditation, fasting, ritual observances, gemstones and other practices. The ethical question is not simply whether a remedy belongs to tradition. The more important question is how it is presented to the client. If a practice is offered as a spiritual discipline, symbolic practice or traditional recommendation, the client can make an informed choice. If it is presented as the only guaranteed way to prevent death, divorce, bankruptcy or disease, the same practice can become an instrument of fear.  A particularly responsible astrological consultation should therefore distinguish between possibility, interpretation and certainty. Language matters. “This period may traditionally be interpreted as demanding greater caution” is fundamentally different from “you will definitely suffer a major disaster.” The first statement leaves room for human agency and uncertainty. The second can create panic and may cause a person to make irrational decisions. The ethical astrologer should understand that confidence of expression is not evidence of certainty.  This principle also changes the role of prediction. Prediction can become useful when it is treated as an invitation to reflection rather than a sentence imposed upon the future. If an astrological interpretation suggests a period traditionally associated with professional pressure, the practical response might be to review finances, improve professional skills, avoid unnecessary risks and communicate carefully. These actions have value independently of whether the astrological interpretation ultimately proves correct. In this model, astrology becomes a framework for contemplation rather than a substitute for judgment.  The same principle applies to relationships. Marriage astrology and compatibility analysis are popular areas of consultation in India, and public listings for Pandit Ajay Gautam show services including Janam Kundli and Kundali Matching. An ethical approach should never reduce another human being to a numerical score or declare a relationship doomed solely because of an astrological combination. Compatibility involves communication, values, emotional maturity, mutual respect, financial expectations, family circumstances and countless other human factors. Astrology, for those who believe in it, may provide one interpretive perspective, but it should not erase the actual people involved.  The same caution becomes even more important in health-related matters. An astrologer should never encourage a client to abandon medical diagnosis or treatment because a chart supposedly explains a disease. Astrology may have a spiritual or reflective role for a person, but medical questions belong to qualified medical professionals. The ethical boundary protects both the client and the credibility of the astrological practice itself. A responsible astrologer should be willing to say, in effect, “this is outside the proper scope of astrology.”  Financial decisions require a similar discipline. A chart should never be presented as a guaranteed investment strategy. Claims that a planetary position guarantees wealth, a particular trading outcome or the success of a business transaction can expose vulnerable people to serious financial harm. Traditional astrological consultation may be used by some people as a reflective tool when considering career or business questions, but real financial decisions should also consider evidence, risk, market conditions, professional advice and the individual’s financial capacity.  The ethical astrologer therefore occupies an unusual position between tradition and modernity. On one side is an ancient body of symbolic knowledge that many people find spiritually meaningful. On the other side is a modern world increasingly shaped by scientific reasoning, evidence, psychology, financial literacy and individual autonomy. The challenge is not necessarily to force one worldview to destroy the other. The challenge is to prevent either worldview from being misused.  Pandit Ajay Gautam’s public profile reflects this attempt to combine traditional astrological concepts with a more contemporary, client-oriented style. His published material describes his work as extending beyond routine horoscope reading into counseling and practical guidance, while his professional profile identifies areas including Vedic astrology, numerology, palmistry and Vastu. Independent business listings also show that he has been offering astrology-related services in Madhya Pradesh and has received substantial numbers of user ratings, although such listings and testimonials should be understood as evidence of public customer feedback rather than scientific validation of predictive accuracy.  This distinction between reputation and verification is essential. An astrologer may have thousands of satisfied clients, extensive experience and a strong public reputation. Those facts can demonstrate popularity, professional reach or customer satisfaction, but they do not by themselves establish the scientific accuracy of astrological predictions. An intellectually honest article about astrology should make that distinction explicit. Respect for an astrologer’s work does not require pretending that every astrological claim has been scientifically proven.  Indeed, the strongest case for ethical astrology may be made not by claiming absolute certainty but by accepting uncertainty openly. An astrologer who says that an interpretation has limits can actually appear more credible than someone who promises perfect predictions. Human life is extraordinarily complex. Birth circumstances, education, personality, family relationships, social conditions, economic opportunities and individual choices interact continuously. No responsible consultation should pretend that a human being can be reduced completely to a birth chart.  This is where the idea of logic-driven astrology becomes particularly significant. Logic does not necessarily mean rejecting every traditional practice. It means examining claims carefully, separating observation from interpretation, distinguishing probability from certainty and refusing to manufacture fear for commercial advantage. It means asking whether a recommendation is proportionate to the problem, whether the client understands what is being suggested, and whether the advice preserves the person’s freedom to make an independent decision.  Ethical consultation also requires financial transparency. A client should know the consultation fee before beginning, understand whether additional services cost extra, and never be pressured into purchasing expensive remedies. The public listing for one Pandit Ajay Gautam service, for example, displays consultation pricing, illustrating the broader importance of making commercial terms visible to clients. Transparency is not merely a business courtesy; in a field involving emotionally vulnerable clients, it is part of professional ethics.  Another important principle is the rejection of guaranteed miracles. Gautam’s own AstroZon material explicitly warns people to be cautious of anyone promising instant solutions or miraculous outcomes, emphasizing that astrology should provide guidance rather than operate as a magic solution. This principle deserves much wider attention because it places responsibility back where it belongs: on the individual, whose decisions, effort, character and circumstances remain important regardless of astrological interpretation.  A non-fear-based astrologer can therefore become less like a fortune-teller delivering an irreversible verdict and more like an interpreter helping a person think about patterns, timing and possibilities. The consultation becomes a conversation. The astrologer interprets the traditional system; the client supplies the lived reality; and the final decision remains with the client. This model is considerably healthier than an authoritarian relationship in which every event is attributed to planets and every solution requires another payment.  There is also a psychological dimension to this approach. People naturally search for patterns when confronted with uncertainty. Astrology can provide a narrative structure through which individuals examine their experiences. Whether one accepts the underlying astrological claims or regards astrology primarily as a symbolic tradition, the reflective process can encourage people to ask meaningful questions about priorities, relationships, fears and future goals. But that potential benefit is weakened when consultation increases anxiety instead of reducing it.  The rebellion against superstition should therefore not be confused with a rebellion against faith. Spirituality can coexist with critical thinking. A person can believe in prayer while consulting a doctor for an illness. A person can value a birth chart while reviewing financial risks before making an investment. A person can follow a traditional ritual while refusing to believe that failure to perform it will inevitably cause tragedy. The mature position is not necessarily absolute acceptance or absolute rejection; it is the ability to maintain discernment.  For Pandit Ajay Gautam, this distinction forms an important part of the identity he presents publicly. His own published descriptions emphasize ethical practice, practical remedies, empathy and the avoidance of fear-based tactics. His public writings also frame astrology as something that can help people understand life rather than simply frighten them about the future. Whether every individual agrees with the astrological framework itself, the ethical principles behind such an approach are broadly understandable: honesty, transparency, proportionality, personal responsibility and respect for the client’s freedom.  Ultimately, the future of astrology may depend less on increasingly dramatic predictions and more on the quality of the relationship between practitioner and seeker. The public is becoming more informed, more skeptical of exaggerated claims and more capable of comparing information from different sources. In such an environment, an astrologer who relies exclusively on fear may gain attention temporarily, but an astrologer who respects the intelligence and autonomy of clients has the possibility of building a more sustainable form of trust.  The real “superstition rebellion,” then, is not the destruction of astrology. It is the destruction of the assumption that spirituality requires fear, that tradition requires unquestioning obedience, or that uncertainty gives someone else the right to control another person’s choices. It is a call for astrology to become more transparent about its nature and limitations while preserving the cultural and spiritual meanings that its practitioners and followers value.  An ethical astrologer does not need to tell a client that destiny is hopeless. The more constructive message is that a chart, within the traditions of astrology, may be interpreted as describing tendencies, periods or possibilities, while human beings continue to exercise judgment and make choices. Such an approach transforms the consultation from a frightening declaration of fate into an opportunity for reflection.  That is ultimately the most compelling idea behind an ethical, non-fear-based approach to astrology associated with Pandit Ajay Gautam: the astrologer should not become the master of the client’s future. The astrologer should become an interpreter, a guide and, where appropriate, a source of perspective. The client should leave with more understanding rather than more dependency, more courage rather than more anxiety, and more responsibility for life rather than less.  In that sense, the rebellion against superstition is also a rebellion against exploitation. It asks astrology to meet a higher ethical standard: interpret without intimidating, advise without controlling, recommend without coercing, respect tradition without abandoning reason, and acknowledge uncertainty rather than disguising it as certainty. Whether one approaches astrology as spiritual wisdom, cultural heritage, symbolic interpretation or a personal belief system, these principles can create a consultation environment based on dignity and informed choice.  The strongest astrologer, under this philosophy, is therefore not necessarily the person who claims to know everything that will happen. It may be the person who understands the limits of prediction, communicates those limits honestly and still helps the seeker find a constructive path forward. That is where astrology can move away from superstition and toward a more reflective, responsible and humane form of consultation.

2 Corinthians 11:8 Commentary Verse Quoted in KJV “I robbed other churches, taking wages of them, to do you service.” 2 Corinthians 11:8 Detailed Exegesis of Each Natural Phrase “I robbed other churches,” Paul continues the argument of verse 7, where he asked, “Have I committed an offence in abasing myself that ye might be exalted, because I have preached to you the gospel of God freely?” Now he explains how he was able to minister in Corinth without requiring financial support from the Corinthians themselves: “I robbed other churches.” Obviously Paul is not confessing literal theft. The man who commanded honesty, refused covetousness, provided things honest “in the sight of men,” and took elaborate precautions in handling church money is not casually admitting that he burglarized congregations to finance missionary travel. The statement is deliberate, forceful irony. Other churches supported him while Corinth received the immediate benefit of his labour. The expression makes the contrast deliberately uncomfortable. Other churches gave; Corinth received. Other believers carried some of the financial load while Paul laboured among people who were not carrying that load themselves. Philippians 4:15–16 supplies the historical background: “no church communicated with me as concerning giving and receiving, but ye only,” and, “even in Thessalonica ye sent once and again unto my necessity.” Second Corinthians 11:9 will add that “the brethren which came from Macedonia supplied” what Paul lacked. He calls this “robbing” because, in a figure, he was taking resources from one field so he could labour freely in another. He did not steal their money; he accepted their sacrifice so Corinth could receive what Corinth was not paying to receive. There is a quiet rebuke in that sentence. The Corinthians had become impressed with false apostles who boasted, promoted themselves, and apparently knew how to exploit religious status, while Paul had made personal sacrifice to avoid burdening Corinth. The irony is almost painful. The man they questioned had cost them less while giving them more. The men they admired looked impressive while Paul had worked with his hands and received help from churches elsewhere. Religious flesh has always had an odd ability to distrust the servant who sacrifices and admire the salesman who invoices. The phrase also shows that churches may participate materially in ministry occurring beyond their immediate location. The Macedonian believers were not merely paying for benefits inside their own congregation. Their gifts helped Paul preach somewhere else. Gospel fellowship crosses geography. A church may support missionaries, evangelists, Bible work, church planting, relief, or other faithful ministry without personally seeing every immediate fruit. A dollar given in Macedonia could become a sermon preached in Corinth because Christian stewardship can travel farther than the hand that releases it. “taking wages of them,” Paul clarifies what he means by “robbed”: he was “taking wages of them.” That phrase is important because it proves once again that receiving material support for gospel ministry is not inherently carnal, greedy, or unspiritual. Paul calls the support “wages.” First Corinthians 9:14 had already stated, “Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.” First Timothy 5:18 says, “The labourer is worthy of his reward.” The New Testament recognizes that genuine ministry involves labour and that those labouring may legitimately receive material provision. That destroys the crude argument that a preacher is automatically compromised because he receives a salary. Paul sometimes worked with his hands, sometimes received support from churches, and sometimes deliberately refused support from a particular church because circumstances made refusal wiser for the testimony. The Bible does not give us one mechanical financial arrangement

sample_tweets.text: I'm currently of the mind that it doesn't have to be anonymous as it isn't meant to contend with something like TOR. However 2 hosts operating in the walled garden shouldn't being able to correlate that a user on both of their platforms is the same person. There are some strategies I've heard brainstormed to mitigate non-anonymity but it isn't the problem I want to solve right now. (Not that it isn't important mind you.)  And I'm 100% sure that hosts on the network should not be able to boot people out of the walled garden. I don't intend to give more power to large sites, more take the burden of moderation off small ones. Of course if a user is violating rules of the walled garden (sharing an identity with other people, running unannounced scrapers) that would be grounds for losing access.  I wouldn't want to impose how moderation of a particular host must be done, if they want to ban for particular opinions that's their own (bad) choice. It can't be opinionated on things outside its 'jurisdiction' lest hosts and users won't have incentive to use it.  Hosts should also be allowed to accept connections from outside the walled garden, provided they don't forward those connections into it arbitrarily, or perform arbitrary lookups on their behalf. That would defeat a lot of the utility. This is probably essential to obtain a userbase, it would fracture the web. Right now non-normies are forced to use platforms that normies are on. If the walled garden required hosts reject all connections from outside of it, it would just be immediately killed and non-normies would never have the opportunity to join.  Hosts could still choose whether they support external connections or not, arbitrarily turning it on and off depending on what's happening. Sudden DDOS attack? Just turn off the unprivileged portal. Obviously Cloudflare already does a lot of this so there isn't a huge inventive. But it should be trivial from a technical perspective.  Hosts that don't care to cater to normies and would rather sacrifice quantity for quality would likely opt to operate totally within the walled garden.  Part of my goal is to bring communities that have slipped off the open web into their own smaller walled gardens, back into the open. Forums for example are a big example.   Touching on non-anonymity again, part of my thoughts on it are that outside of using a VPN we are already effectively not anonymous. Governments can subpoena it in the snap of a finger. I'm hoping this design would still allow one to connect to the walled garden using a VPN, but they would still need a 'personalized' id which would need to be turned over. If they did everything right, all that would reveal about them is their VPN connection and the vouch chain for the identity.  Speaking of that, I'm pretty strongly of the opinion the right mechanism for this is vouches. The reason is that if an individual vouches for too many bad actors, they can lose vouch privileges, and everyone they vouched for retroactively needs new vouches to access the garden. This would ripple down, and up, the chain. The principle here is that you can't just vouch for anyone because it reflects back on you. I intend for people to think about who they vouch for, whether they trust them to follow the rules or not.  I initially played with this idea as a way of preventing cheating in online games. I'm sure some of the design reflects that.  It should be obvious, while it isn't anonymous, it wouldn't require government ID to participate. Online games also made it clear that doesn't work anyway, in Korea elderly people just sell their ID to kids, they make a new account and start cheating again.  It isn't infallible but it increases the cost of making sock puppet accounts greatly. That should ultimately be the goal, increase the cost of turnover. The detail most people miss in the Wyoming story: this money funds schools.  FRNT is a state-issued digital dollar, fully backed by cash and short-term U.S. Treasuries. By law, the yield on those reserves goes to Wyoming’s School Foundation Program.  Then April happened.   North Korea’s Lazarus Group breached the node infrastructure behind LayerZero’s verifier, forged one message, and pulled $292 million out of KelpDAO’s bridge. Wyoming’s cross-chain vendor had just been taken apart by a nation-state.  For a DeFi protocol, that’s a risk to price in. For a state managing citizens’ property and a school fund, it’s disqualifying. The security review ended with a first in U.S. history: a government entity publicly replacing its blockchain infrastructure. LayerZero deprecated across all eight chains FRNT runs on, from Ethereum to Solana. Chainlink CCIP, exclusive, multi-year contract.  Nearly $15 billion migrated for business reasons. Wyoming migrated for its citizens.

DeFi security's biggest shift in 2026 — three of the four largest exploits this year weren't smart contract bugs at all, they were access compromises, and the numbers point at who's behind most of them.  DeFi lost over $840M to hacks so far this year. The number that actually matters isn't the total, it's what caused it.  Three of the four largest incidents in 2026 didn't involve a single flawed line of Solidity. The smart contracts did exactly what they were programmed to do. They executed instructions from someone who had obtained access they shouldn't have had.  That's a different problem than the one most audits are built to catch. A code audit checks whether the logic is correct. It doesn't check whether the private key, the multisig signer, or the admin account that can call that logic is actually still under the right person's control.  Chainalysis attributes roughly 76% of crypto hack losses globally this year to Lazarus Group and other state-linked actors. These aren't opportunistic exploiters scanning for a reentrancy bug. They're running long social-engineering campaigns to get inside the access layer, sometimes over months, before touching a single contract.  If your protocol's security review only covers the code, it's reviewing the part that's already working correctly. The part that's failing is who can sign, who can call admin functions, and how you'd know if that access changed hands.

💡 O PDF de US$ 600 Milhões  Em 2022, um grupo de hackers roubou US$ 600 MILHÕES de uma empresa de tecnologia. Eles não quebraram nenhuma criptografia avançada. Eles usaram apenas um arquivo PDF com uma proposta de emprego irrecusável. 🧵👇  A Sky Mavis era a criadora do jogo Axie Infinity, o maior fenômeno de Web3 da época, movimentando bilhões de dólares em tokens através de sua rede própria, a Ronin Bridge.  A segurança da rede era mantida por 9 nós validadores. Para conseguir aprovar um saque fraudulento, um hacker precisaria invadir simultaneamente pelo menos 5 desses nós — algo considerado praticamente impossível.  Mas os hackers do Lazarus Group não tentaram invadir os servidores. Eles invadiram a mente dos funcionários.  Usando o LinkedIn, eles criaram uma empresa fantasma de recrutamento e entraram em contato com um engenheiro sênior da Sky Mavis.  Após várias rodadas de entrevistas falsas, disseram que ele havia sido aprovado com um salário astronômico. Para oficializar, enviaram a "proposta oficial" em um arquivo PDF.  O arquivo, na verdade, continha um malware espião (spyware). Assim que o engenheiro baixou e abriu o documento no seu computador de trabalho, os invasores ganharam acesso total aos sistemas internos da empresa.  Com o controle da máquina, os hackers rastrearam as chaves privadas e assumiram o controle de 4 nós validadores da rede. Pouco depois, encontraram uma brecha em uma autorização antiga e dominaram o 5º nó necessário.  Em poucos minutos, eles sacaram 173.600 Ethereum e 25,5 milhões de USDC da ponte. Foi o maior hack da história da Web3 na época: US$ 620 milhões sumiram sem disparar um único alarme imediato.  💡 A lição para a tecnologia e para o cotidiano:  A maior vulnerabilidade de qualquer sistema de segurança digital nunca é o código criptográfico: é a confiança humana.  O hacker moderno raramente quebra a porta da frente; ele apenas descobre como fazer alguém abrir a porta por dentro.  #Tech #Web3

DeFi's Worst Quarter Ever: $775 Million Gone in Three Months, and Hackers Have Changed How They Work  DeFi has lost $942 million to 121 hacks in the first half of 2026. Q2 alone accounts for 85 of those incidents and roughly $775 million in losses, per CryptoRank on-chain data, making it the most active exploit quarter the industry has ever recorded. That's a 70% increase over the same window last year.  The numbers are bad. The method shift is worse.  🔓 How the attacks changed  Smart-contract bugs used to be the headline risk. Audits were the answer. That framework is now incomplete. Social engineering and compromised infrastructure have overtaken code exploits as the primary loss vector in 2026, the first time that's happened. Attackers aren't hunting for a Solidity error anymore. They're targeting the humans and systems that sit above the code.  Chainalysis attributes approximately 76% of 2026's crypto hack losses to actors linked to North Korea's Lazarus Group, which has consistently favored credential theft, phishing, and supply-chain compromise over pure technical exploits. The numbers reflect that preference at scale.  🌉 Bridges keep taking the hits  Cross-chain infrastructure remains the most expensive single attack surface in DeFi. Bridge TVL hit $21.94 billion as of March 2026, according to CryptoRank. Cumulative bridge losses since 2022 now exceed $2.8 billion. The capital concentration hasn't shrunk, and neither has attacker interest in it.  DeFiLlama pegs all-time exploit losses across crypto at over $16.5 billion, with DeFi-specific losses near $7.7 billion. Those figures were built incrementally, one protocol at a time, but 2026 is stacking losses fast.  🧯 Aave's rsETH freeze and what it showed  When Kelp DAO was breached earlier this year, Ethereum adjacent markets felt it immediately. Aave froze rsETH markets on both V3 and V4, despite its own contracts being untouched. The protocol was collateral damage. That's the contagion dynamic that audit-only security frameworks don't address. One governance-layer or operational failure at a connected protocol becomes everyone's problem.  Against all of this, TRON and Hyperliquid were the only top-10 chains to grow TVL in 2026, up roughly 5% and 7% respectively. The broader DeFi TVL trend, as Finextra noted, is still pointing down. Capital is concentrating in fewer places, which means the targets are getting bigger even as the total pool shrinks.  ▪️Tickers: ethereum:native   ethereum:0x7fc66500c84a76ad7e9c93437bfc5ac33e2ddae9  tron:native  hyperliquid:native

sample_tweets.text: Berlin state ministries got cut off from Germany's central government IT network this week after a security breach. Not a minor hiccup. A disconnection significant enough that someone decided the right move was to sever the link entirely, which is the cyber equivalent of containing a fire by pulling down a wall.  No attribution confirmed yet, and we should be honest that confirmed attribution takes time. But let's talk about context, because context is doing a lot of work here.  Germany has been a documented Russian cyber target for years. APT28, also known as Fancy Bear, has been identified by both the BfV (German domestic intelligence) and the BND (foreign intelligence) as a persistent threat to German government networks, political parties, and critical infrastructure. The German government, along with EU and UK partners, has formally co-attributed a Russian FSB cyberattack on Poland's power grid. Russian disinformation campaigns targeting Germany ahead of federal elections have been confirmed by security services as centrally orchestrated from Russia. This is not a theoretical threat landscape. It is a documented, named, ongoing one.  So when Berlin state ministries get isolated from central government IT infrastructure, the question of who did it is not idle speculation. It sits inside an established pattern.  The targeting choice is worth thinking through carefully. State-level ministries in a federal system are an interesting pick. They're not the highest-profile targets, but they're also frequently not as well-resourced defensively as federal infrastructure. They hold sensitive administrative data, internal communications, coordination records. And critically, they're connected to the larger government network, which makes them a potential pathway into that network if the attacker's goal is lateral movement rather than just disruption. The fact that isolation protocols were triggered suggests whoever is managing incident response took that possibility seriously. You don't cut off a ministry from the central network because things look manageable.  This fits a pattern we've been tracking across European governmental infrastructure. Russian military intelligence has been documented using compromised IP cameras to surveil NATO logistics movements. The FSB hit Polish power infrastructure. These aren't one-offs. They're a persistent, grinding campaign against alliance member state systems at multiple levels, federal, state, critical infrastructure, private sector adjacent to government. The variation in targeting keeps defenders spread thin.  The state-level focus specifically deserves more attention than it usually gets. Federal agencies get the security investment and the political attention. State and regional government networks in EU member states are frequently the weak link, and adversaries with enough patience and resources to map out a federal system's architecture know exactly where the softer entry points are. Germany's federal structure means sixteen states, each with their own administrative networks, each a potential approach vector.  The timing matters too. Germany just came through a federal election cycle that attracted significant documented Russian interference activity. Hybrid operations in the Russian playbook don't tend to end cleanly when an election concludes. Cyberattacks combined with disinformation are designed to compound each other: the attack creates a real disruption, the disruption generates news coverage and political noise, and disinformation campaigns shape how that noise is interpreted. The goal isn't just the breach. It's the surrounding effect.  What we don't have yet: confirmed attribution, clarity on which ministries were affected and what data may have been accessed or exfiltrated, and a full picture of how the breach occurred. Forensics takes time and governments are often reluctant to release details that reveal how they were penetrated. So this post will have gaps that only time and official disclosure can fill.  What we do have: a significant enough incident that emergency isolation protocols were activated, occurring in a European capital, against government infrastructure, during a period of well-documented heightened Russian hybrid operations against NATO member states. The operational profile is consistent with previously confirmed Russian APT activity. That doesn't make it confirmed. It makes it the leading hypothesis worth treating seriously while investigation proceeds.  The broader catalog is getting long. Hacked cameras watching NATO supply lines. Power grid attacks. Political party network intrusions. Election interference campaigns. And now Berlin ministries cut off from central government IT. European state-level government networks are being tested repeatedly, and the results of those tests keep suggesting the same thing: the resourcing and defensive posture at sub-national government level across the EU is not keeping pace with what's being thrown at it.  That gap is the actual strategic problem. Individual incidents get covered. The systemic vulnerability underneath them gets a paragraph, maybe two, and then we move on.  foreigninterference.org/post… #foreigninterference #AdvancedPersistentThreatOperations #CyberEspionage #InfrastructureAttacks #PersistentNetworkInfiltration

🚨 Hackers Are Poisoning Hotel Wi-Fi to Steal Microsoft 365 Accounts  ReliaQuest has uncovered a widespread campaign targeting Wi-Fi infrastructure at hotels, conference centers and other shared venues, allowing attackers to redirect travelers to malicious Microsoft 365 infrastructure without compromising their devices or sending phishing emails.  * The campaign has been active since at least June 2026  * Compromised Wi-Fi gateways were identified across multiple U.S. cities as well as India and Saudi Arabia  * Attackers gain administrative control of captive-portal gateways and manipulate DNS responses  * Once a gateway is compromised, users connecting to that Wi-Fi network can be silently redirected to attacker-controlled infrastructure  * ReliaQuest observed Microsoft-themed domains being used to facilitate credential and account compromise  * In some cases, attackers abused Microsoft's device-code authentication flow, potentially obtaining MFA-satisfied Microsoft 365 access through valid OAuth tokens  * WPAD abuse was also attempted in roughly one-third of observed cases, potentially allowing additional application traffic to be routed through attacker-controlled proxies  * Victims connecting to affected gateways came from financial services, legal, healthcare, energy, retail and professional-services organizations  🇷🇺 ReliaQuest says the techniques overlap with tradecraft previously associated with APT28 / Fancy Bear / Forest Blizzard, the Russian military intelligence-linked threat group.  However, researchers are NOT directly attributing this campaign to APT28 because they have not identified direct technical links such as shared infrastructure or code reuse.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: This attack changes the traditional phishing model. The employee doesn't need to click a malicious email or connect to an obviously suspicious website. Compromising infrastructure that users already trust allows attackers to move the interception point from the endpoint to the network itself.  For corporate travelers, ReliaQuest's primary recommendation is straightforward: enforce an always-on, full-tunnel VPN so DNS traffic passes through trusted corporate infrastructure rather than the hotel gateway.  Source: ReliaQuest Threat Research reliaquest.com/blog/threat-s… #DDW #CyberSecurity #ThreatIntelligence #APT28 #Microsoft365

5/𝗰𝗲 𝗾𝘂’𝘂𝗻 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗲́𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗮𝗶𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝘂 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗲𝘂 𝗱𝗲 𝟲𝟬𝟬 𝟬𝟬𝟬 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘀 Imaginons maintenant un scénario hypothétique. Un service étranger n’a pas besoin de connaître les 678 000 dossiers. 👉Il recherche peut-être seulement : 50 militaires ; 30 diplomates ; 100 chercheurs ; 200 ingénieurs ; quelques hauts fonctionnaires ; des spécialistes du nucléaire ; des collaborateurs d’entreprises de défense. 👉La base fiscale lui permet éventuellement de connaître : -adresse personnelle, -situation familiale, -revenu, -patrimoine immobilier, -téléphone, -courriel. 👉Une autre fuite permet d’obtenir : -IBAN, -banque, -date de naissance. Une autre : -enfants, -établissement scolaire. Une autre : -administration d’appartenance. 👉Le service peut alors lancer une attaque extrêmement ciblée. Pas contre 600 000 personnes. Contre une seule. C’est ainsi que des données massives deviennent du renseignement de précision. Encore une fois : 👉il s’agit d’un scénario de risque, pas de la description d’une opération russe démontrée dans l’affaire ZeroBytes. 𝗹𝗮 𝗴𝘂𝗲𝗿𝗿𝗲 𝗵𝘆𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝘂𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗹𝗮 𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗲 𝘃𝗼𝗹𝗲 𝗹𝗮 𝗺𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲́𝗲 Il existe enfin un dernier scénario souvent oublié. Une puissance étrangère peut exploiter politiquement un scandale qu’elle n’a pas créé. Supposons que tous les pirates soient français et purement criminels. Les incidents restent réels : -FICOBA compromis. -ANTS compromis. -Tchap compromis. -DGFiP compromise. -Éducation nationale compromise. Un dispositif d’influence étranger peut simplement amplifier ces informations en répétant : « L’État français est incapable de protéger ses citoyens. » Puis : « Ils vous cachent la vérité. » « Toutes vos données ont été volées. » « Votre gouvernement ne contrôle plus rien. » Certaines phrases peuvent partir de faits exacts puis être progressivement exagérées. Le but n’est pas nécessairement de faire croire à une histoire entièrement fausse. 👉Les opérations d’influence les plus efficaces utilisent souvent une vérité réelle comme point de départ, avant d’y ajouter peur, exagération et suspicion. La cyberattaque devient alors seulement la première étape. La véritable cible devient : -la confiance dans les institutions. La diplomatie française considère précisément les cyberopérations russes comme une composante d’un ensemble de menaces hybrides associant cyberactivité, manipulation de l’information et ingérence dans les processus démocratiques. 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟳 𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗲́𝗷𝗮̀ 𝗱𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗲̂𝘁𝗲𝘀 La prochaine élection présidentielle française doit se dérouler en 2027. Le communiqué français du 13 juillet 2026 concernant le FSB mentionne explicitement la volonté de la France de contrer les opérations de déstabilisation, y compris à l’approche des élections de 2027. 👉Pourquoi ? Parce qu’une opération moderne peut prendre la forme d’un hack-and-leak. -On pirate. -On récupère des documents. -On attend. Puis on publie au moment politiquement le plus destructeur. Le danger devient encore plus important lorsque des documents authentiques sont mélangés à quelques documents falsifiés. L’existence d’une énorme quantité d’informations vraies rend alors les faux beaucoup plus difficiles à identifier. La France possède déjà l’expérience de 2017 et attribue désormais au GRU l’utilisation d’APT28 dans les tentatives de déstabilisation de ce processus électoral. Voilà pourquoi les immenses bases de données volées ne doivent pas être regardées uniquement à travers le prisme de la fraude bancaire 𝗼𝘂̀ 𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗼𝗻𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗲𝗻𝗾𝘂𝗲̂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝘂𝗷𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗱’𝗵𝘂𝗶 ? Pour la DGFiP, une plainte a été déposée et les investigations continuent afin de déterminer précisément l’étendue des extractions. La CNIL a été saisie. Pour l’Éducation nationale, une plainte contre X a été déposée auprès du parquet de Paris ; l’ANSSI et la CNIL ont également été saisies. Le ministère confirmait encore le 18 août 2026 que l’enquête judiciaire se poursuivait et que les expertises concernant les éventuelles données d’élèves n’étaient pas terminées. Pour Tchap, la DINUM poursuit l’analyse des journaux techniques afin de déterminer le périmètre exact des consultations et des données éventuellement exfiltrées. Pour ANTS, l’enquête judiciaire a permis d’identifier au moins un auteur ; le gouvernement évoque le jeune suspect âgé de quinze ans. Les vulnérabilités ont été corrigées ou font l’objet d’un plan de remédiation sous accompagnement de l’ANSSI. Et pour ZeroBytes, l’identité réelle complète des personnes se trouvant derrière le pseudonyme et surtout celle des acheteurs revendiqués restent les grandes inconnues publiques du dossier. 𝗰𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗹𝗮 𝗰𝗻𝗶𝗹 𝗽𝗲𝘂𝘁 𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗿𝗲́𝘃𝗲́𝗹𝗲𝗿 La CNIL joue ici un rôle différent de celui de la police. La justice cherche notamment : 👉qui a attaqué ? La CNIL cherche également : les responsables des fichiers avaient-ils mis en place un niveau de sécurité suffisant ? Après une violation, elle peut examiner : -les mesures de protection, -la gestion des habilitations, -la conservation des informations, -la détection de l’incident, -la rapidité de la réaction, et la manière dont les victimes ont été averties. 👉Ce point sera particulièrement important. Car le véritable scandale ne serait pas seulement qu’un pirate ait réussi à entrer. Il faudrait également déterminer si certaines faiblesses étaient connues, prévisibles ou auraient raisonnablement pu être évitées. 𝗰𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗶 𝘃𝗮 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗿𝗲 𝘃𝗶𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗻𝗲 La conséquence la plus immédiate de ces fuites n’est probablement pas spectaculaire. 👉Elle est psychologique. Jusqu’à aujourd’hui, lorsqu’un interlocuteur connaissait notre adresse, notre situation fiscale ou une partie de notre dossier administratif, nous pouvions raisonnablement penser : « Il doit réellement travailler pour l’administration. » Ce raisonnement devient dangereux. 👉Le fait qu’une personne connaisse désormais -votre adresse, -votre IBAN, -votre revenu fiscal, -votre enfant, -votre établissement scolaire, ou votre numéro fiscal 👉ne prouve plus qu’elle représente l’organisme dont elle prétend venir. À mesure que les bases se multiplient sur les marchés clandestins, notre ancienne méthode pour distinguer le vrai du faux — « il connaît des informations confidentielles, donc il est légitime » — devient obsolète. 👉C’est peut-être l’un des changements les plus profonds provoqués par cette crise. 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻  𝗟𝗘 𝗦𝗖𝗔𝗡𝗗𝗔𝗟𝗘 𝗡’𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗣𝗟𝗨𝗦 𝗦𝗘𝗨𝗟𝗘𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗤𝗨𝗘 𝗡𝗢𝗦 𝗗𝗢𝗡𝗡𝗘́𝗘𝗦 𝗔𝗜𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗘́𝗧𝗘́ 𝗩𝗢𝗟𝗘́𝗘𝗦. 𝗟𝗘 𝗦𝗖𝗔𝗡𝗗𝗔𝗟𝗘 𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗤𝗨𝗘 𝗡𝗢𝗨𝗦 𝗜𝗚𝗡𝗢𝗥𝗢𝗡𝗦 𝗤𝗨𝗜 𝗙𝗜𝗡𝗜𝗥𝗔 𝗣𝗔𝗥 𝗟𝗘𝗦 𝗣𝗢𝗦𝗦𝗘́𝗗𝗘𝗥. Il faut maintenant regarder l’ensemble. 👉Fin janvier 2026 : FICOBA est consulté frauduleusement après l’usurpation des identifiants d’un fonctionnaire.  👉Environ 1,2 million de comptes bancaires sont concernés. 15 avril 2026 : l’ANTS détecte une intrusion susceptible de concerner 11,7 millions de comptes ; quelques jours plus tard, le ministre de l’Intérieur parle d’environ 11,6 millions de données nominatives exfiltrées. 👉30 avril : le Premier ministre reconnaît environ trois vols de données par jour, une importante dette numérique, des systèmes remontant parfois aux années 1990 et une perméabilité croissante entre acteurs criminels, individus et puissances étrangères. 👉7 juin : un compte Tchap est compromis ; 73 467 agents publics sont potentiellement concernés. 👉25 juillet : nouvelle intrusion à l’Éducation nationale. 👉12 et 13 août : la compromission des systèmes de la DGFiP devient publique ; 678 000 particuliers et professionnels apparaissent dans le premier bilan. 👉La FAQ du fisc révèle ensuite que les informations potentiellement récupérées comprennent bien davantage que le seul revenu fiscal : identifiant fiscal, état civil, téléphone, courriel, situation familiale, personnes à charge, nombre de parts, revenu fiscal de référence, taux de prélèvement à la source et historique des échanges avec l’administration. Et pendant que tout cela se produit, la France accuse officiellement le GRU russe d’avoir utilisé APT28 contre des intérêts français et désigne le 16e Centre du FSB, unité 61240, comme menant des opérations persistantes de cyberespionnage contre notre pays. 👉Voilà pourquoi le dossier est infiniment plus sérieux qu’un simple « piratage du site des impôts ». Il révèle trois crises simultanées. 👉La première est technique : l’État possède encore une dette numérique considérable. 👉La deuxième est criminelle : la donnée personnelle est devenue un marché. 👉Et la troisième est géopolitique : des puissances étrangères cherchent activement à pénétrer les systèmes français et peuvent s’appuyer sur des acteurs non étatiques dans leurs opérations. Il ne faut pas fabriquer un coupable pour rendre l’histoire plus spectaculaire. Nous n’avons aucune preuve que ZeroBytes travaille pour Moscou. C’est précisément parce que le dossier est suffisamment grave sans inventer quoi que ce soit qu’il faut rester rigoureux. Mais nous devons désormais nous poser une question différente. 👉Pas seulement : « Qui a volé ces données ? » Mais : Qui les a copiées ? Qui les conserve ? Qui les revend ? Qui les rachète ? Qui les recoupe avec d’autres bases ? Qui sélectionne certaines personnes ? Qui peut les exploiter dans cinq ans ? Parce qu’une base numérique n’est pas comme un camion rempli de documents. Le camion ne peut être vendu qu’une fois. Une base peut être copiée mille fois. Un pirate peut la vendre aujourd’hui à un fraudeur. Demain à un courtier. Après-demain à un autre criminel. Et rien n’empêche théoriquement qu’une copie finisse un jour entre les mains d’un acteur ayant des motivations entièrement différentes. C’est là que la frontière entre cybercriminalité et sécurité nationale devient dangereusement mince. Nous avons confié à l’État des informations que nous ne confierions probablement jamais toutes ensemble à une entreprise privée : nos revenus, notre domicile, nos comptes, notre patrimoine, notre famille, nos enfants, notre identité. Nous l’avons fait parce que le fonctionnement d’un État moderne l’exige. Mais ce choix repose sur un contrat implicite : l’État collecte parce qu’il protège. Lorsque la protection faiblit, ce contrat de confiance commence à se fissurer. Et il existe une différence fondamentale entre l’argent et l’identité. 👉L’argent volé peut parfois être remboursé. Une carte bancaire peut être remplacée. Un mot de passe peut être changé. Mais personne ne peut changer son passé. Personne ne peut remplacer sa date de naissance. Personne ne peut effacer facilement ses anciennes adresses. Personne ne peut changer le nom de ses enfants. Personne ne peut réinitialiser vingt années d’histoire administrative. C’est pourquoi le véritable héritage de ces attaques peut nous poursuivre beaucoup plus longtemps que leurs auteurs. La grande bataille numérique qui commence ne porte donc pas seulement sur des serveurs. Elle porte sur notre capacité à rester maîtres de notre identité

The Pentagon has defended the action, stating it is part of its broader BOND (Business Operations for National Defense) budget planning to optimize the defense industrial base and track ammunition or vehicle supply chain delays.  The MSS, powered by Palantir’s algorithms, has served as the digital backbone for Ukrainian artillery and drone operations. The software ingests raw data from thousands of commercial satellites, battlefield sensors, radar, and social media geolocations. Within seconds, it spits out precise coordinate targets for artillery crews. Pentagon officials credited Maven with compressing the time it takes to find and strike an enemy vehicle from hours down to minutes.  Following its success in active combat zones, the Pentagon has integrated Project Maven into its Combined Joint All-Domain Command and Control (CJADC2) framework in the Pacific. The system is currently monitoring Chinese naval movements in the South China Sea, predicting ship movements, and automatically alerting U.S. and allied naval commanders to anomalies in shipping lanes.  Before Palantir stepped in and built the Maven Smart System (MSS), the task of processing battlefield data and identifying targets was handled by a mix of traditional tech giants, defense contractors, and highly manually-driven legacy software.  The primary systems before AI-driven Project Maven were heavy, siloed databases where human analysts had to do the heavy lifting manually. Giants like Raytheon, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, and General Dynamics built the military's legacy Command and Control (C2) systems.  Palantir explicitly optimizes its battlefield software to run on top of both Microsoft Azure and AWS government clouds.  Microsoft has used its exclusive partnership with OpenAI to deploy secure, air-gapped Large Language Models (LLMs) inside classified military networks. This allows commanders to use conversational AI to query troop logs or maintenance schedules, a direct challenge to Palantir's text-based data querying tools.  That is interesting to me because Claraview was founded in 2001 by Sid Banerjee, Justin Langseth, and Nithi Vivatrat (my former CPO who has long served on POGO's board). Claraview's business intelligence and data warehousing consultancy was later acquired by Teradata in 2008.  Teradata has a deep, long-standing global partnership with Microsoft. While their relationship dates back decades to business intelligence and database interoperability, it has evolved into a strategic cloud and artificial intelligence alliance.  In April 2026, Teradata launched its enterprise-grade Analyst Agent on the Microsoft Marketplace. This allows Azure clients to purchase and deploy Teradata's conversational AI tools directly through their existing Microsoft commercial cloud agreements. Reflecting the strength of the relationship, Teradata named Microsoft its Americas Partner of the Year.  Teradata and its core data analytics products have widespread military, defense, and national security applications. The company maintains a dedicated subsidiary—Teradata Government Systems—which actively contracts with the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD), international defense ministries, and the intelligence community.  By ingesting data streams from drones, satellites, and radar feeds, Teradata’s platform helps military operators construct an AI-driven decision chain to rapidly isolate threat patterns and reduce target-response times.  However, Sid and Nithi financial exited Teradata with the closing of the sale 18 years ago. They immediately shifted their focus to building and scaling Clarabridge, a text analytics spin-off they had incubated, which was where I met them.  Conceptually, Clarabridge's core capabilities fit the definition of dual-use technology, because natural language processing (NLP) and sentiment analysis can be applied to both commercial and intelligence tasks. However, commercially and regulatory-wise, Clarabridge itself was not classified or restricted as a dual-use weapon or espionage tool.  But the exact same algorithmic concepts—parsing massive streams of unstructured text, tracking user sentiment, mapping network behavioral nodes, and performing real-time linguistic monitoring—are heavily utilized by defense agencies and psychological operations (PsyOps) divisions for open-source intelligence (OSINT), threat monitoring, and tracking adversarial digital propaganda.  Clarabridge never faced the heavy defense export controls or "dual-use" regulatory hurdles typically applied to aerospace or encrypted defense software for several practical reasons. Unlike Teradata (which explicitly maintains a federal defense subsidiary to support military aviation logistics and battlefield connectivity), Clarabridge focused almost entirely on consumer brands, financial services, healthcare, and hospitality markets.  Microsoft and Palantir maintain a deep, specialized partnership to deliver AI and analytics to the U.S. defense community. However in the commercial corporate market, Microsoft's Azure/Copilot tools and Palantir's AIP platforms routinely battle each other to be chosen as the central data backbone for Fortune 500 corporations.  When broader geopolitical threats loom, the two companies routinely team up. For instance, Microsoft and Palantir jointly spearheaded an alliance of major tech companies pushing back against heavy government restrictions on AI deployment, aiming to maintain American technological dominance over foreign adversaries.  But this is a bit of a tangent so I want to pivot back to an earlier point.   The FBI kept Crossfire Hurricane so tightly compartmentalized that even within the U.S. DOJ, only about five high-level officials were initially aware of its existence.  Declassified reporting indicated that UK diplomats later requested the U.S. to ensure specific redactions were maintained on declassified "Russiagate" documents to protect shared intelligence methods and safeguard the US-UK diplomatic relationship.  By law (50 U.S.C. § 3091), the IC must keep the congressional intelligence committees "fully and currently informed" of significant intelligence activities. If an agency hid an operationalized technological breakthrough from the executive command while briefing unauthorized outside figures, it would likely violate statutory congressional reporting laws.  While it is rare for an agency to brief Congress on a major operational breakthrough without also informing the sitting President (who is their boss), it is not inherently illegal. If POTUS chooses not to receive certain briefings, does not ask, or if the agency determines the President does not have an immediate operational "need to know" for a specific localized project, notifying Congress alone fulfills their statutory legislative duty.  Two of the most senior intelligence officials in the US and UK privately shared concerns about “our strange situation” as the FBI launched its 2016 investigation into whether Donald Trump’s campaign was colluding with Russia, the Guardian reported on 30 July 2019.  Those text messages were between Andrew McCabe, the deputy director of the FBI at the time, and Jeremy Fleming, his then counterpart at MI5, now the head of GCHQ. During his period as a senior official at MI5, Fleming served as director for intelligence collection and led MI5’s preparations for the 2012 Olympics. He was appointed deputy director of MI5 in 2013.  Jeremy Fleming and British intelligence agencies like MI5 and GCHQ were not involved in investigating the Russian state-sponsored sports doping scandal in 2014. However, they became heavily involved in the subsequent international security response when Russian's GRU began hacking the global anti-doping bodies.  Furious over being exposed and banned from major athletic competitions, Russia launched a aggressive cyber-espionage and disinformation campaign. The GRU (specifically Fancy Bear / APT28) targeted WADA, the International Olympic Committee (IOC), and the U.S. Anti-Doping Agency (USADA). They stole and leaked the private medical records of Western athletes.  In 2013, Kara Goucher and fellow whistleblower Steve Magness formally brought their evidence to USADA. The FBI formally stepped into the investigation in early 2017. The overall investigation into the Nike Oregon Project effectively closed in October 2019. CYBERATTAQUES : CE QUE CHRISTINE KELLY OUBLIE SUR LA GUERRE HYBRIDE RUSSE  « Une honte pour notre pays », écrit Christine Kelly après le vol de données fiscales concernant 678 000 personnes et professionnels. L’attaque est grave. Les défaillances doivent être expliquées. Mais une journaliste ne transforme pas un fait en slogan national sans enquête, comparaison ni attribution.  Commençons par la vérité qui dérange les deux camps : à ce jour, aucun élément officiel rendu public ne permet d’attribuer les intrusions visant la DGFiP ou l’Éducation nationale au Kremlin. Affirmer le contraire serait malhonnête. Mais prétendre que la guerre hybride russe contre la France est une invention le serait tout autant.  En avril 2025, le Quai d’Orsay a officiellement attribué au renseignement militaire russe, le GRU, plusieurs cyberattaques menées par APT28. Depuis 2021, une dizaine d’entités françaises — services publics, entreprises privées et organisation liée aux Jeux de Paris — ont été ciblées ou compromises. Paris rattache aussi à cette unité le sabotage de TV5Monde en 2015 et la tentative de déstabilisation de l’élection présidentielle de 2017.  En juillet 2026, l’ANSSI a documenté les opérations de Turla, liées au FSB : ministères, diplomatie, défense, justice et technologie françaises ont été visés depuis des années. Son Panorama 2025 rappelle que les acteurs étatiques ciblant les intérêts français pour l’espionnage et le prépositionnement sont principalement liés à la Russie et à la Chine.  Et le cyber n’est qu’un volet. VIGINUM a recensé 77 opérations informationnelles du réseau russe Storm-1516 entre fin 2023 et mars 2025. Leur but : discréditer des institutions et personnalités occidentales, manipuler l’opinion et fournir des récits parfois repris, consciemment ou non, par des figures influentes. L’Union européenne décrit la même mécanique : cyberattaques, sabotage, atteintes aux infrastructures et manipulation de l’information.  Voilà la guerre hybride : la cyberattaque fracture le système ; la propagande fracture la confiance. Le Kremlin n’a pas besoin d’être derrière chaque piratage. Il lui suffit d’exploiter chaque faille pour marteler le même récit : État incapable, démocratie en ruine, France « toujours pire qu’ailleurs ».  On peut débattre de la réponse à apporter ; on ne peut plus sérieusement présenter cette guerre hybride comme un fantasme.  Madame Kelly, je ne vous accuse pas de recevoir des ordres de Moscou. Je constate que vos formules — « toujours en France », « honte pour notre pays » — reprennent exactement ce cadrage sans apporter la moindre comparaison internationale. Or une journaliste établit les faits, cherche les responsables et contextualise. Une éditorialiste distribue la honte.  La France doit corriger ses failles et exiger des comptes. Mais elle doit aussi regarder qui l’attaque, qui amplifie ses vulnérabilités et qui transforme chaque crise en preuve de son effondrement. La lucidité n’est ni du complotisme ni de la russophobie. C’est la première défense d’une démocratie.

Operation Aurora hit Google in late 2009. That's the one most people remember from that year, and it's a reasonable anchor point, but it undersells how much was actually happening across the board in U.S. counterintelligence during that period.  The Defense Personnel Security Research Center put out a comprehensive look at foreign espionage patterns targeting the United States in 2009, and reading it now, you can see the architecture of problems that would define the next decade of CI work taking shape in real time.  Start with the cyber piece, since Aurora is the headline. The attack on Google and a range of other major corporations wasn't just notable for its targets. It demonstrated that state-sponsored actors had reached a level of technical capability where they could sustain persistent access inside major private sector networks over extended periods, running long-term collection operations rather than smash-and-grab intrusions. The malware involved was sophisticated enough that forensic attribution took time, and the operational patience involved, sitting quietly inside networks and pulling data, was a signal about where this was heading. Foreign intelligence services weren't just trying to steal a document. They were trying to build ongoing visibility into systems, communications, and R&D pipelines. Aurora gets called a watershed moment a lot, and it earns that description.  But the cyber operations were happening alongside something older and more traditional: direct recruitment of Americans with access to classified information. FBI counterintelligence assessments from this period documented multiple cases of foreign services actively targeting cleared personnel. The recruitment playbook hasn't changed much in sixty years. Financial pressure is probably the most reliable lever. Someone who's underwater on debt, going through a divorce, or facing some kind of financial crisis is a target of opportunity, and foreign intelligence services are patient and methodical about identifying those vulnerabilities. Ideological sympathy is another vector, and professional grievance is a third: the person who feels passed over, disrespected, or wronged by their employer or by the government. Foreign services are good at finding those people and being very understanding about it.  The economic intelligence side of the picture is where the 2009 assessment connects most directly to what the National Counterintelligence Executive was tracking through the 2009-2011 window. The focus wasn't just on classified military or government information. Adversaries were going hard after trade secrets and proprietary technology in strategic commercial sectors. The coordination between state intelligence services and commercial entities is the part that makes this structurally different from Cold War espionage. A foreign government doesn't just want your defense secrets anymore. It wants your pharmaceutical research, your semiconductor manufacturing processes, your aerospace engineering, your energy technology. And it has corporate proxies, front companies, and state-linked firms that can absorb that stolen IP and turn it into competitive advantage in global markets. The line between economic espionage and state intelligence collection had essentially dissolved.  The reason this 2009 assessment matters beyond just being a historical document is that it captures a moment of transition. The patterns it identified, cyber-enabled collection at scale, persistent network intrusions into private sector targets, systematic recruitment exploitation of personal vulnerabilities, and state-directed economic espionage through commercial channels, were all still developing. The U.S. counterintelligence community was watching these vectors mature in real time and trying to figure out how to respond to threats that didn't map cleanly onto the Cold War framework most of the institutional infrastructure had been built around.  Aurora was prosecuted as a Chinese state operation targeting Google's source code and, separately, the Gmail accounts of Chinese human rights activists. Both tracks matter. The source code theft is the economic and technical espionage piece. The activist surveillance is the transnational repression piece. Both came out of the same operation, which tells you something about how integrated these objectives were on the adversary side. This wasn't a single-mission operation. It was a multi-objective collection effort wrapped in a single intrusion campaign.  The personnel security vulnerabilities piece of the 2009 picture is worth sitting with for a minute because it's the part that gets the least attention and probably causes the most sustained damage. Cyber intrusions are dramatic and generate headlines. A single recruited asset with sustained access to classified information over years can be more valuable to a foreign service than any network penetration. The Aldrich Ames and Robert Hanssen cases from earlier decades had made this point catastrophically clear, and the 2009 assessments showed that foreign services hadn't stopped trying. If anything, the financial crisis of 2008-2009 had expanded the pool of potentially vulnerable personnel. People who had been financially stable were suddenly not. People who had relied on certain assumptions about their economic future were watching those assumptions collapse. Foreign intelligence services notice that kind of thing. They read the same economic news everyone else reads.  What the Defense Personnel Security Research Center was documenting in 2009 was a threat environment that had multiple simultaneous dimensions operating at different speeds. Cyber operations could compromise a network in weeks. A recruited human source could provide access for years. Economic espionage through commercial proxies could transfer competitive advantage across an entire industrial sector over a decade. Each of these required different detection methods, different responses, and different institutional frameworks. The challenge for U.S. counterintelligence was that the adversaries had figured out how to run all three tracks at once, and the American system was still largely organized to handle them separately.  The 2009 period also sits at an interesting point in the evolution of the U.S.-China CI relationship specifically. Aurora would eventually be attributed to a Chinese military unit. The economic espionage patterns documented by NCIX pointed heavily at Chinese state-linked collection efforts. This wasn't the full-blown, publicly-acknowledged strategic competition framing that became standard by the late 2010s. In 2009, there was still significant institutional reluctance in parts of the U.S. government to be direct about the source and scale of Chinese intelligence operations, partly for diplomatic reasons and partly because the economic relationship made it complicated. The counterintelligence community's internal assessments were clearer about what they were seeing than the public posture of the government often suggested.  The systematic nature of what DPSERC documented is the key word in understanding why this period matters. Individual espionage cases had always existed. What 2009 revealed, taken together, was a pattern of coordinated, multi-vector intelligence collection that was systematic in a way that suggested strategic direction rather than opportunistic targeting. Foreign services weren't just taking what they could get. They were running organized campaigns against specific sectors, specific technologies, specific categories of personnel.
